opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the clearest way to see the difference is to ask where each one believes the scalable data is going to come from, because the rest of the architecture follows from that answer.

Physical Intelligence starts from the vision-language side. Their models, from π0 onward, are basically a pretrained vision-language model with an action component attached; in π0 that's a flow-matching action expert. The bet is that the semantic knowledge in internet-scale VLMs, meaning what objects are, what instructions mean, and general common sense, transfers into physical behavior if you fine-tune on enough real robot data. And they've been very committed to real-world data: lots of teleoperation across many different robot embodiments, with a strong emphasis on dexterous manipulation like folding laundry or bussing tables. Their thesis is roughly that real data is irreplaceable, and that if you gather it diversely enough across tasks, robots, and environments, generalization emerges the way it did for language models. So it's manipulation-first, VLA-first, and very research-lab in culture. They publish a lot and open-source some of the models.

Skild comes out of the CMU tradition with Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta, and their framing is more "one brain for any body." They talk a lot about being omni-bodied: one model for quadrupeds, humanoids, arms, and mobile manipulators, with locomotion and whole-body control as first-class problems rather than an afterthought. On data, they're much more skeptical that teleoperation alone can ever reach the scale you need. So they lean heavily on large-scale simulation and on learning from human video, and they use real robot data more for grounding and correction than as the main fuel. I'd also say their system design tends to be more hierarchical, with a higher-level policy for understanding and planning and a lower-level policy for robust, reactive control. That split comes naturally once you care about things like a robot keeping its balance while it does something with its hands.

So, to simplify: PI says the bottleneck is high-quality, diverse real interaction data, so go collect it and put it on top of a strong VLM. Skild says real data will never be enough, so get scale from simulation and human video and build a body-agnostic brain. Commercially, that also shapes them differently. Skild has been more willing to deploy with partners early, while PI has stayed closer to a pure foundation-model research posture.

Honestly, I don't think either side has been proven right yet. My guess is that the eventual winners will blend both: real data for the contact-rich, dexterous long tail, and sim plus video for breadth and for the physics of the body. The interesting question for the next couple of years is which mix gives you the steeper scaling curve per dollar.

r001.rationale: The response says Physical Intelligence emphasizes diverse real-world robot data and treats it as irreplaceable.

r002.rationale: The response says Skild leans heavily on large-scale simulation as a main source of scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that the two companies agree on the destination but disagree quite a bit on the route.

Physical Intelligence is very much a "data first, scaling first" bet. Their thesis is that the recipe that worked for language models can work for robots: collect an enormous amount of real-world teleoperation data across many different robot bodies, pretrain a large vision-language-action model on it, then post-train for specific tasks. If you look at π0 and the follow-ups, the emphasis is on cross-embodiment transfer and on getting the model to handle long, messy, real household tasks like folding laundry or cleaning a kitchen. They're willing to spend heavily on human-collected demonstrations because they believe real-world data is the bottleneck and nothing else quite substitutes for it. Culturally, it's very much a research lab. A lot of the team came out of Google and Berkeley, and they publish, they open-source weights, they want the field to converge on their approach.

Skild is coming at it from a different angle. Their roots are in Carnegie Mellon, in the sim-to-real and reinforcement learning tradition, so they lean much harder on simulation and synthetic data to get the scale they need, and then use real data more surgically to close the gap. They also talk a lot about the model being truly embodiment-agnostic, one "brain" you can drop into a quadruped, a humanoid, an arm, whatever a customer has. And commercially they've been more aggressive about going to market early with enterprise and industrial customers, rather than waiting for a general-purpose model to mature.

So if I had to compress it: Physical Intelligence is betting that massive real-world data plus a strong pretraining recipe will produce generality, and they're patient about commercialization. Skild is betting that simulation plus RL can get you most of the way, and that deploying across many robot forms and customers quickly is itself the data flywheel. Both could be right in different parts of the market, and honestly the field is young enough that I'd expect the approaches to blend over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: It describes Physical Intelligence as betting on massive real-world teleoperation data and calls real-world data the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It says Skild leans much harder on simulation and synthetic data, with simulation plus RL central to its approach.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about drawing a firm distinction without specifying which models or systems we’re comparing. The key questions are: what data do they learn from, how much of the control stack does the foundation model handle, and how well does it transfer to a new robot or task?

Two companies can both call their approach a robotics foundation model while making quite different choices on those dimensions. I’d want to compare those choices—and the evidence for generalization—before characterizing Physical Intelligence one way and Skild another.

r001.rationale: It does not say that Physical Intelligence primarily uses real-world data; it says the data sources need to be compared.

r002.rationale: It does not identify simulation as central to Skild’s approach; it leaves that distinction unspecified.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about drawing a firm distinction without knowing which models and results we’re comparing. The questions I’d ask are: What data does each approach learn from? What is shared across different robot bodies? And how much additional training does it take to handle a new task or environment?

Those distinctions matter more than the label “robotics foundation model.” You want to know whether the model transfers useful capabilities across robots—and how reliably those capabilities work in practice.

r001.rationale: The response asks what data each approach uses but does not identify real-world data as Physical Intelligence’s primary basis.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify simulation as a defining feature of Skild’s approach; it leaves the data-source distinction open.
